# OpenAI Private Intelligence: ZDR safety review is rolling out, Private Inference is still a preview


By OpenTools Team


DevDay gave OpenAI's privacy work one name, but its two pieces have different release states. An API buyer also needs to distinguish zero OpenAI retention from 30‑day encrypted safety records in customer storage.


##


DevDay brought two privacy efforts under one name


[OpenAI's September 29 DevDay recap](https://openai.com/index/devday-2026-recap/) introduced Private Intelligence as a way for businesses to use its models with stronger data controls. The name groups an API safety‑processing configuration with a separate Private Inference preview. Those are not two generally available products a buyer can switch on today.


The chronology matters. OpenAI[previewed Private Safety Processing in August](https://openai.com/index/offering-zero-data-retention-for-frontier-models/) , as[TechCrunch reported at the time](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/19/openai-seeks-to-one-up-anthropic-with-new-customer-privacy-protections/) . OpenAI updated its announcement on September 22 to say the API rollout had begun in phases. DevDay did not mark its first reveal. What the event added was the Private Intelligence umbrella and a stated fall preview of Private Inference, which OpenAI says will combine confidential computing with verifiable controls. The recap provides no broad availability date or complete technical specification for that future inference layer.


##


Zero OpenAI retention does not mean zero safety storage


For an approved API project,[Zero Data Retention](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data) excludes customer content from OpenAI's abuse‑monitoring logs and treats the` store` setting on Responses and Chat Completions as false. Endpoint‑specific application state and input exceptions still need checking. ZDR with Private Safety Processing adds an automated way to examine patterns across interactions without routine OpenAI‑personnel access to their underlying content. That is OpenAI's documented architecture, not an independent OpenTools security test.


The[technical guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/private-safety-processing) says a classifier referral or approved sampling policy selects a prompt‑and‑response record; a referral by itself is not a violation. The record is encrypted and written asynchronously to the customer's regional cloud storage. OpenAI keeps an operational index and storage reference, rather than a copy of the content. An approved hardware‑attested runtime is designed to decrypt selected records for automated safety review and release only predefined, bounded safety signals and operational metadata in plaintext. Detailed results remain encrypted in customer storage.


OpenAI specifies a **30‑day time to live** for those encrypted retained safety records. This reconciles the seemingly conflicting terms: OpenAI says it does not retain the prompts and responses in its own ZDR abuse logs, while selected records do persist temporarily in storage the customer controls. Customer‑managed encryption is an additional recommended control; revoking its authorization can prevent later decryption but does not erase a stored record or undo a review already completed. The[data‑controls guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data) also notes that image and file inputs flagged for possible child sexual abuse material can be retained for manual review even under ZDR. A buyer should not describe the entire arrangement as absolute non‑retention or a universal no‑human‑review guarantee.


##


The project policy and storage health are the operating checks


OpenAI's[PSP setup guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/private-safety-processing) says organizations already approved for ZDR can configure customer‑controlled AWS, Azure or Google Cloud storage, then register and validate it for an API project. Once enabled, the PSP policy applies to all API traffic in that project, including requests to models that would not otherwise require PSP. A team that needs plain ZDR for eligible models must use a separate project configured accordingly. Registering storage alone leaves the current policy unchanged until validation succeeds.


Validation is a configuration check, not continuous proof that a bucket or access grant works. The guide tells administrators to monitor provider activity and health separately. The[endpoint eligibility table](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data) is another boundary: some features may retain application state even when ZDR is set. Before adopting the new configuration, an enterprise architect should document which project, endpoints, region, storage lifecycle, access grants and current validation/health status apply to the actual workload. Those checks are more actionable than treating “private” as one setting shared across every product.


##


Private Inference remains a separate later decision


The[DevDay recap](https://openai.com/index/devday-2026-recap/) describes Private Inference as a preview **coming this fall** , not a capability available as part of today's PSP setup. It says the work combines confidential computing with strict, verifiable controls, but does not yet supply the deployment, attestation, threat‑model and customer‑eligibility details needed to compare it with an existing inference environment. It would be premature to count on those properties for a present procurement or compliance decision.


The useful decision today is narrower: determine whether phased ZDR with PSP access covers the relevant API endpoints, where selected encrypted safety records live for 30 days, who controls retrieval and decryption, and how the project shows its active policy. Watch for a separate Private Inference specification and rollout before making claims about that future layer. The announcement belongs to[OpenAI](https://opentools.ai/organizations/openai) ; it changes a data‑control boundary rather than introducing a new model.
